items.action: Brito Aranha describes the Tagus's numerous, varied shipping, naming moinhos, rascas, faluas, moletas, fragatas, varinos, botes, catraios, canoas and others; most carried lateen sails.
items.boat: moinhos, rascas, faluas, moletas, aveiros, fragatas, hiates,

items.action: The rasca sails out over the bar to load figs at Algarve ports.
items.conditions: leaves river navigation, goes beyond the bar

items.action: The moleta, used in fishing, is also rigged as a hiate to carry out some commercial commission.
Some boats were used only for river navigation, called navigation of the Ribatejo.
Most of these boats came from the Barreiro and Seixal shipyards, whose residents also commonly formed their crews; Trafaria residents supplied most fishing crews.
items.who: residents of Barreiro, Seixal and Trafaria

items.action: The largest boats with the most crew came from shipyards at Esposende, Figueira, Porto and other northern coastal towns.
Boats are rigged with lateen sails, either two masts or one, as on the varino.

Each Portuguese coastal or riverside area built its own typical boats; on the Tagus these include muletas, bateiras, enviadas, faluas, fragatas, canoas and botes, with specialised names spreading from the Discoveries era.
items.boat: muletas, bateiras, enviadas, faluas, fragatas, barcos de águ
items.period: from the era of the Discoveries

items.action: Until roughly the Discoveries, 'barca' was a general term for any small river-traffic or fishing boat on the Tagus.
The 1190 Foral of Almada mentions the 'barca do pescado'; Fernão Lopes's chronicle mentions Almada barcas alongside ships loading wine and salt for export.
items.boat: barca do pescado, barcas de Almada

numbers.what: year of the Foral of Almada

items.action: Many ships, said to number seventy to eighty at each spot, lay loading salt and wine near Sacavém and Montijo; crowding forced barcas to land at Santos.
items.conditions: dense crowding of ships before the city left no room to maneuver
items.place: rio de Sacauem, ponta do Montijo, Santos

items.action: Portuguese Discoveries ships changed over the 15th and 16th centuries, from round-sailed barcas to larger lateen-rigged barinéis and caravels, later adapted and improved.
Portugal began the Discoveries enterprise with the conquest of Ceuta.
From the early 16th century, Tagus boats generically called barca began to diversify by function and by route.
Shipbuilders in riverside towns built shallow-draught boats without keel or with half keel for going upriver and navigating the river's shallow arms.
items.boat: embarcações de pequeno calado, sem quilha ou de meia quilha
items.conditions: shallow river arms and upriver navigation
items.place: Porto Brandão, Margueira, Mutela, Amora, Arrentela, Seixal, Barreiro, Gaio, Sari

items.action: Shipyards also existed at other Tagus ports upriver.
items.place: Valada, Punhete (Constância), Rossio ao Sul do Tejo (Abrantes)

items.action: The Regimento dos Barqueiros listed the river traffic boat types: barca, batel, caravelão, muleta and bateira; the muleta then carried cargo rather than fished.
The regulation refers to barcas, caravelões, batéis and muletas loading bulk straw, oven firewood and similar goods.
A number of river boats, barcas and batéis, served the city of Lisbon, while many naus and caravels entered Lisbon's port each year.

numbers.what: naus and caravels entering Lisbon yearly

items.action: Nicolau de Oliveira mentioned barcas used in sea fishing, from Alfama, Cascais, Sesimbra, Setúbal, Peniche and Ericeira, showing fish abundance.
items.place: Alfama, Cascaes, Cezimbra, Setuual, Peniche, Eyriceira

items.action: Growing river traffic from Portuguese expansion's logistical needs boosted shipbuilding and created new boat types, varying also by each shipyard or riverside town's style.
Formerly, fragatas, varinos, faluas, botes, canoas and catraios with sails, paint and crews animated the Tagus riverside, documented in engravings, photos and texts.
items.boat: fragatas, varinos, faluas, botes, canoas, catraios

items.action: During the 20th century the Tagus lost most of its nautical heritage; muletas, bateiras, faluas and other types almost disappeared.
items.boat: muletas, bateiras, enviadas, faluas, fragatas, barcos de águ

items.action: Fragatas and varinos survived almost to the present; botes and canoas of Sarilhos Pequenos and Moita survive thanks to a small group of enthusiasts.
Riverside municipalities preserved and reused some surviving boats for cultural purposes.
items.place: Seixal, Moita, Alcochete, Vila Franca de Xira, Azambuja

items.action: A photograph caption shows a bote de fragata belonging to the Seixal municipal ecomuseum at Valada.
A figure caption shows a boat being hauled by towing from the riverbank while passing the Cachão do Cabril rapids.
